newsitem.title: USA: Florida emergency managers decry hurricane cuts.
newsitem.headline: Florida emergency managers decry hurricane cuts.

text.p: Florida emergency managers told the nation's top weather official Wednesday that budget cuts at the National Hurricane Centre could lead to costly false alarms and unnecessary evacuations.

County emergency management directors, in a meeting with National Weather Service director Joe Friday, said cuts at the hurricane centre could compromise confidence in the center's predictions and may result in mistakes that will cost communities millions of dollars in evacuation costs.
In addition, emergency managers said, false alarms may erode public confidence in evacuation orders, putting more residents in harm's way.

Friday, who met with local managers at the behest of Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles, said $27.5 million in cuts to the agency's budget will be felt at the Miami-based National Hurricane Centre, where 15 positions ranging from part-time clerical positions to three scientific posts were cut.
The Atlantic hurricane season begins June 1.
The cuts worry emergency planners, who rely on hurricane centre forecasts to determine whether to evacuate, a procedure that officials say costs $1 million per mile of coastline.

"We need the very latest information before we can make that final and sometimes fatal decision to issue an evacuation order," Palm Beach County emergency coordinator B.T Kennedy said. "Anyone who says that they can maintain the same high level of service and still reduce their staff is untruthful."

Friday, whose agency is requesting $10.8 million in supplemental funding to bolster its budget, said the system is now safe. But he added that without supplemental funding, federal lawmakers may be putting citizens' lives at risk.

The supplement would fund employee training, equipment maintenance and spare parts, but would not affect the decision to cut staff at the hurricane centre or close the southern regional headquarters in Fort Worth, Texas in 1999.
The facility, which coordinates activities from New Mexico to Florida, will be melded into other divisions.

"I understand that every mistaken forecast from now on will be blamed on this decision," Friday said. "But I want you to remember that even with the best, most accurate forecasting done ...we'll still miss one to two storms out of 10."
